_comment: Hand-maintained page content. Read src/data/README.md before editing: it says who reads the page, what each field is for, and how to check the result. `npm test` validates the structure.
name: Cale McCammon
intro:
These are my public projects. The recent ones are a Kotlin-to-Lua compiler, a Go alerting service over Postgres, an Android app whose screens an AI agent lays out, an Android weather app also built in six cross-platform frameworks, batch and streaming data pipelines, a text-to-SQL benchmark, and Flutter and React Native apps. The older repositories, from 2018 on, are Android and Java.

Six are described below. The rest are in the repository list at the bottom of the page.

featured.summary: A compiler from Kotlin to plain, readable Lua. It targets Lua 5.1 to 5.4 and LuaJIT, and runs as a command-line tool or a Gradle plugin.
points: Parsing and type checking go through the Kotlin Analysis API. Kotlin that k2l cannot translate is a compile error.
The output needs no third-party Lua code. The compiler copies in only the parts of its own Lua runtime that a program uses.
252 golden test programs are compiled and run on all five Lua interpreters in CI, and ten more cases check the compiler's error messages.

featured.summary: A native Android weather app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose: a map, place search, saved places, a home-screen widget and notifications of severe weather. Forecasts are kept in Room and refreshed in the background by WorkManager, so the app opens on its last place with no connection. The same app is also built in six cross-platform frameworks, kmp-weather and flutter-weather among them.
points: Room is the one source of truth. A fetched forecast is written to the database and never returned to the caller, so the screens, the Glance widget and the background worker all read the same rows and none has to be told when another has fetched.
The build is 16 Gradle modules whose shared settings live in convention plugins. A feature module depends on the domain and the shared UI only, so it cannot name Room, Retrofit or the other feature.

178 JVM tests include Compose tests of both screens and screenshot comparisons. Six more run the whole app on an emulator in CI against a stand-in weather server, with WorkManager's test driver running the scheduled refresh that Hilt builds.

featured.summary: An Android app where you ask about ten US stocks and the economy, and an AI agent answers with a native Jetpack Compose screen of figures, charts and rankings. The agent, in Python with FastAPI, lays the screen out in the A2UI protocol and streams it over Server-Sent Events; the data comes from the dbt marts of data-engineer-finance-analytics.
points: The model never writes a number. It calls six typed tools that run fixed SQL, the agent stores each result in the screen's data model, and the model binds components to those paths. A layout that writes a figure itself or binds to a path that is not in the data is rejected and sent back once for correction.

Every A2UI message is stored in Room as it arrives and the screen is drawn from what is stored, so a conversation comes back after a restart with the agent down. The Python and Kotlin halves are tested against the same catalog and against answer streams recorded from the agent.

Run against qwen3:8b on a laptop GPU, the model called the right tools for 47 of 50 questions, but only 1 answer passed the A2UI SDK's validation; the rest fell back to a plain message, so nothing broken reached the screen.

featured.summary: A streaming pipeline for live crypto trades. A producer reads the Binance.US WebSocket into Redpanda, a consumer lands the trades as Parquet, and DuckDB builds one-minute candles that dbt turns into incremental gold tables. Dagster runs the batch steps.
points: Kafka offsets are committed only after the trades they cover are in a Parquet file, and each file is written under a temporary name and then renamed. A killed consumer re-reads what it had not flushed, and the next stage never reads part of a file.

Late trades are handled by re-reading a trailing 90-second window, rounded down to the minute because candles are replaced whole. The watermark is kept per symbol, so a symbol whose backlog arrives behind another's is not passed over.

The rolling-window dbt models compute their windows over every candle and filter afterwards, so a re-emitted row never gets a shortened window. One test builds silver and gold from Parquet files through the Dagster assets, which puts every dbt model and test in CI.

featured.summary: Delay alerts for Finnish cargo rail. A Go service over Postgres polls an open rail API on a schedule and sends one alert per watch rule, train and day, however many polls see the delay.
points: Duplicate suppression is a UNIQUE constraint with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so two overlapping poll runs cannot both send the same alert.
Sign-in is GitHub OAuth with no scopes requested, and the database stores only a SHA-256 hash of each session token.

Webhook URLs come from users, so the service guards against SSRF: it rejects private addresses, re-checks the IP after DNS resolution, and does not follow redirects. 144 tests cover this and the rest, with the store tests running against a real Postgres.

featured.summary: A benchmark for text-to-SQL models. It runs each generated query against a fixed DuckDB warehouse and compares the rows with the reference query's rows, so differently written but correct SQL still passes.
points: The comparison rules are documented and tested: row order counts only when the reference query has a top-level ORDER BY, rows compare as a multiset, and floats compare within a tolerance.

Generated SQL is treated as untrusted input. It runs in an in-memory DuckDB with external access disabled and a 15-second timeout, and wrong answers are sorted into failure classes such as unknown column, wrong shape and wrong order.
In the committed run, llama3.2 answered 22 of 72 questions correctly. With table names but no column names in the prompt it answered 1 of 24, and 56% of all failures were unknown-column errors.
